notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: In modern Large Language Model (LLM) architecture, what does Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) do, and how does it change cost scaling?
notes.back: MoE routes each token through a small subset of specialist feed-forward (expert) layers via a router, instead of activating all layers. Compute then scales with active parameters, not total parameter count. As of 2026 it is mainstream/baseline (DeepSeek V3, Qwen3-Next, Mistral variants).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: Why is the Key-Value (KV) cache used during LLM inference, and what is its main cost?
notes.back: It stores the Key and Value matrices for already-processed tokens so attention does not recompute them each step, cutting latency. Cost: cache size grows linearly with context length. Above ~128K tokens the KV cache can exceed parameter memory (e.g. Llama 70B at 1M ctx ≈ 135 GB at FP16, more than its weights).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: Compare Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA).
notes.back:
MQA: all query heads share one Key/Value head — up to ~32× KV compression but ~1-3 pt quality regression.
GQA: query heads share KV in groups — balance of efficiency/quality; default in Llama 3, Mistral.
MLA (DeepSeek): stores a low-rank latent projection of K/V — ~7-14× KV compression, the 2026 efficiency endgame.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: What KV-cache (Key-Value cache) optimizations dominate production LLM serving in 2026?
notes.back: PagedAttention (vLLM memory management), prefix caching (vLLM / SGLang RadixAttention — reuse KV for shared prompt prefixes), attention compression (MQA/GQA/MLA), and quantization (INT8, FP8, NVFP4). Combined they cut long-context cost ~4-40×.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: What is the "lost in the middle" effect and why is it architectural, not a prompt-quality bug?
notes.back: Attention is distributed unevenly: tokens at the start (primacy) and end (recency) of the context get disproportionate attention, while information in the middle is underweighted (reports cite ~40% degradation at scale). It follows from how attention works, so you mitigate it by ordering critical content near the edges, not by rewriting it.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: Name production-ready million-token context windows as of late 2025 / 2026.
notes.back: Gemini 2.5 Pro (~2M tokens), Claude Sonnet 4 (~1M), open-source Qwen2.5-1M. Practical cost: ~15 GB KV cache per user at 1M tokens; prefill latency can exceed 2 minutes at max length.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: What did DeepSeek V4 (April 2026) demonstrate about LLM architecture direction?
notes.back: Not a single radical idea but combining known techniques (hybrid attention + compression) into one system: ~90% KV-cache memory reduction vs prior gen, with extreme context length. Signal: MoE, latent attention, sliding-window are now baseline expectations; the differentiator is execution/efficiency.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: What are RoPE and FlashAttention, briefly?
notes.back:
RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding): encodes token positions by rotating query/key vectors, giving good relative-position behaviour and length extrapolation.
FlashAttention: an IO-aware exact-attention kernel that tiles computation to avoid materializing the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory, speeding up and reducing memory for long sequences.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::01 LLM Architecture
notes.front: What practical risk do MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) systems introduce in production serving?
notes.back: Routing imbalance: tokens routed unevenly to experts cause hot experts, uneven load, and latency spikes that only appear at scale. Hybrid attention/compression similarly makes some inputs hit more expensive compute paths, adding latency variability.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: In Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory, distinguish short-term/working memory from long-term memory by scope.
notes.back:
Short-term / working memory: single-session, within-trial decision context (limited capacity).
Long-term memory: knowledge and experience retained across sessions/tasks (cross-trial), persisting beyond one context window.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: Break down long-term LLM memory into explicit vs implicit, then explicit into its two subtypes.
notes.back:
Explicit (recallable facts/events): episodic = personal experiences/events ("user prefers brand X"); semantic = facts/knowledge about the world.
Implicit: procedural memory — learned skills, strategies, action patterns that guide behaviour.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: List the memory storage paradigms seen across LLM agent systems.
notes.back: Cumulative (append full history), reflective/summarized (periodic compressed summaries), purely textual (natural language), parametric (baked into weights via fine-tune/knowledge editing), and structured (tables, triples, knowledge graphs).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: What is MemGPT and what core idea does it borrow from operating systems?
notes.back: MemGPT treats the LLM like an operating system with virtual memory: hierarchical memory management that pages relevant snippets between short-term (in-context) and long-term (external) stores, using event-driven interrupts to stay coherent over long interactions. (Letta is its productized successor.)

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: How does Mem0 maintain long-term memory, and what is its graph variant?
notes.back: Two stages: extraction (LLM pulls key facts from new turns) then update, where a tool call issues ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP to keep memory consistent. The graph variant (Mem0g) stores entity nodes + relationship edges for complex structure.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: What are the six memory types in MIRIX's multi-agent memory architecture?
notes.back: Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault — each managed by a specialized agent, with a coordinator orchestrating updates and retrieval across them.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: Name several current long-term memory frameworks for LLM agents (2025-2026).
notes.back: Mem0, Zep, Letta (ex-MemGPT), LangMem (LangChain), MemoryOS (OS-inspired short/mid/long tiers), MIRIX (multi-agent, 6 types), A-MEM (agentic memory), MemMachine. Providers (OpenAI, Google) also persist cross-session user memory.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: Per the 2025 position paper (arXiv:2502.06975), what five properties must true episodic memory have?
notes.back: 1) Long-term storage (persists past the session), 2) explicit reasoning over memory content, 3) single-shot learning (captured from one exposure, no gradient update), 4) instance-specific details, 5) contextual binding (who/when/where/why tied to content).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: Why do LLM agents fail at temporal reasoning even when entity recall is good?
notes.back: Retrieval surfaces entities well but chronological awareness (tracking how an entity changes over time) is weak — even strong models score low (e.g. ~0.29 on the 2025 Episodic Memory Benchmark). Mitigation: structured writes tagged with actor/timestamp/entity/trigger/outcome so reads can reconstruct order.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: What is the practical downside of LLM-driven memory extraction (as in Mem0/Zep), and what alternative exists?
notes.back: Relying on the LLM to extract/update/delete adds operational cost, probabilistic-extraction accuracy errors, and compounding error over time. Alternatives (e.g. MemMachine) preserve ground-truth episodic logs and reduce reliance on probabilistic extraction.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: How does "memory" relate to a multi-layer working/episodic/semantic decomposition for long dialogue?
notes.back: Separating working, episodic, and semantic layers (with adaptive retrieval gating + retention regularization) controls cross-session drift and false-memory rate while keeping context growth bounded — better retention than naive cumulative or pure-compression approaches.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::02 Memory Architecture (focus)
notes.front: In the harness view, what burden does the memory subsystem externalize?
notes.back: Memory externalizes state across time, so continuity no longer depends on ephemeral in-context tokens. (Skills externalize procedural expertise; protocols externalize interaction — together they offload burdens the model otherwise can't carry across a window.)

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: Give Anthropic's 2025 working definition of an agent, and contrast it with a workflow.
notes.back:
Agent = an LLM (Large Language Model) autonomously using tools in a loop — you own the goal and guardrails, the model picks the next tool call from environment feedback.
Workflow = LLM/tool calls orchestrated through predefined code — you own the control flow.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: What is the key trade-off of choosing an agent over a workflow?
notes.back: Agents trade predictability for flexibility. Every extra autonomous turn adds latency, token cost, and the chance an early mistake propagates. Guidance: use the simplest pattern that passes eval — often a workflow or one well-tooled call — and reserve agents for paths you can't hardcode but can still verify.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: List Anthropic's five workflow design patterns for agentic systems.
notes.back: 1) Prompt chaining, 2) Routing (send input to a specialized path), 3) Parallelization (sectioning + voting), 4) Orchestrator-Workers (orchestrator decomposes + delegates), 5) Evaluator-Optimizer (one generates, one critiques/refines).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: When is the Orchestrator-Workers pattern the right choice?
notes.back: For tasks of unpredictable complexity where subtasks can't be predefined — e.g. coding agents resolving a GitHub issue across multiple files. An orchestrator dynamically breaks the task down and delegates to workers.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: Contrast pre-inference retrieval with "just-in-time" (JIT) context for agents.
notes.back:
Pre-inference retrieval: embedding-based lookup that front-loads context before the model reasons.
Just-in-time: the agent pulls context during the loop as it discovers what it needs. Modern agentic designs augment retrieval with JIT strategies rather than dumping everything up front.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: Why use sub-agents, and what context property do they provide?
notes.back: Sub-agents give separation of concerns + context isolation: detailed search/work context stays inside the sub-agent, while the lead agent keeps a clean window focused on synthesis. This keeps the lead context small and reduces pollution.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: Name three agentic antipatterns to avoid.
notes.back: Monolithic agents (one giant do-everything agent), over-engineered planning (elaborate planning layers that add cost without payoff), and missing observability (no tracing of steps/tool calls — you can't debug what you can't see).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: What does "reason inside the agent's context window" mean as a design habit?
notes.back: Design from the agent's actual observations (~10-20k tokens/step), not your human priors. A computer-use agent may only get a screenshot + terse task. If that feels fragile, fix it with richer observations (resolution, suggested actions, guardrails), not more orchestration layers.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: What practical checks does Anthropic recommend for diagnosing agent failures?
notes.back: Paste the system prompt into the model and ask what's ambiguous; feed a failed trajectory back and ask why a step failed; run a full task while restricting yourself to only the agent's observations to feel its blind spots.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::03 Agentic Engineering
notes.front: Why start with direct LLM APIs rather than an agent framework?
notes.back: Frameworks hide the prompts and encourage over-engineering. Starting from the raw API keeps the system prompt, tool definitions, and control flow transparent and debuggable; add structure only when evals justify it.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: Define an agent harness and state its core separation of responsibilities.
notes.back: The harness is the deterministic runtime layer wrapping the LLM (Large Language Model). Model proposes actions/tool calls; harness disposes: it validates the schema, checks permissions/budgets/safety, executes, logs, and injects the result back. Without it, agents leak tokens, run uncontrolled loops, and execute dangerous commands.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: What is the cardinal rule about tool execution in harness engineering?
notes.back: Never let the LLM call tools directly. The model returns a structured tool call; the harness validates the schema, checks permissions, executes, and feeds the result back. The model is a stateless token predictor; the harness is the control plane.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: List the core components of an agent harness.
notes.back: The agent loop (call model → parse → execute tools → feed back → decide to stop), tool/function calling (expose + route capabilities, incl. MCP servers), context management (system prompt, history, retrieved docs, compaction/summarization), memory, guardrails, and tracing/observability.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: Describe the "tool cliff" and its practical implication.
notes.back: Agent performance degrades non-linearly as tool count grows (one cited pattern: ~10 tools fine, ~30 degrading, ~107 complete failure). Implication: keep the exposed toolset small and task-scoped; don't bolt on every MCP (Model Context Protocol) server "just in case."

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: How much does the scaffold matter relative to the model, per recent benchmarks?
notes.back: A lot. The same backbone model shows large spreads by scaffold — e.g. SWE-bench Pro ~23% with a basic scaffold vs ~45%+ with an optimized multi-turn one. Scaffold design (orchestration, memory, tool abstractions) is a first-class performance lever, not an afterthought.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: What is the best practice for agent instruction files (e.g. CLAUDE.md / AGENT.md)?
notes.back: Keep them tight and hand-written (~under 60 lines): cover only the decisions the agent commonly gets wrong. LLM-generated instruction files restate the obvious and cost ~20%+ more tokens per call. These files are assembled as first-class "user content" alongside the dynamic system prompt.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: What is "context engineering" and why did it eclipse prompt engineering?
notes.back: Context engineering = deliberately deciding what goes into the context window and in what order (system instructions → memory → tool definitions → history) plus compaction. Per Karpathy (June 2025) it's "the new prompt engineering": arrangement/quality of context drives agent performance more than any single prompt tweak.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: Name four context-engineering techniques a harness can apply to manage the window.
notes.back: Context editing (rule-based pruning), context awareness (tell the model its remaining capacity after each tool call), memory tools (persistent create/read/update/delete files across sessions), and programmatic tool calling (model writes code that calls tools, returning only the final result to the window).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: How does programmatic tool calling reduce context bloat?
notes.back: Instead of issuing many individual tool calls whose outputs all land in the window, the model submits code that invokes tools, consumes intermediate outputs inside the runtime, and returns only the final processed result to the context — cutting tokens on multi-step tool chains.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: For multi-window (long-horizon) tasks, what harness setup improves reliability?
notes.back: Use the first window to build a framework: write tests, create init/QoL scripts, and provide verification tools so the agent can check its own correctness without a human. Have it track progress in structured files and plan before acting.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: What's the standard recommended ordering of the context window?
notes.back: System instructions → relevant memory → tool definitions → conversation history. System prompt should be structured: identity, capabilities, rules, output format — focused and free of contradictions.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::04 Harness Engineering (focus)
notes.front: What transport replaced HTTP+SSE for MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, and why does it matter for harnesses?
notes.back: Streamable HTTP (2025-11-25 spec): client→server via HTTP POST, optional server→client SSE stream over GET. It lets MCP servers run as remote multi-client services rather than local processes — relevant to how a harness wires in and authenticates tools.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: Why must you evaluate agent trajectories, not just final outputs?
notes.back: An agent is a multi-step distributed system; a right-looking final answer can hide bad steps. Score the whole trajectory: tool-choice correctness, argument validity, step count, time/cost, and policy compliance. Use deterministic tool mocks in CI; add judge-based scoring only with a rubric + auditing.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What concrete mechanisms prevent duplicate side effects when an agent retries?
notes.back: Idempotency tokens + deduplication. Classic failure: Agent A times out and retries, Agent B processes a payment twice → double charge despite "correct" per-agent retry logic. Make tool side effects idempotent and dedup at the boundary.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: How should a harness treat retrieved content (web pages, documents, tool output)?
notes.back: As untrusted input. Separate data from instructions (so retrieved text can't hijack the agent — prompt injection), restrict tool permissions, and require approvals for irreversible actions. Model-centric guardrails alone don't fix weak contracts.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: Distinguish guardrails from evaluations in an LLM system.
notes.back:
Guardrails act in real time, blocking unsafe/non-compliant behaviour before output reaches the user.
Evaluations act in batches, measuring reliability/grounding/bias across many prompts or model versions over time. You need both.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What recovery controls belong in a policy-first tool layer?
notes.back: Per-tool-class retry with backoff, circuit breakers (stop hammering a failing tool), bounded retries (never unbounded), risk-aware gating, redaction patterns, and explicit invariants/contracts. Most failures come from weak contracts, missing invariants, no idempotency, and unbounded retries — not the model.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What did Datadog's 2026 data reveal about LLM call failures in production?
notes.back: In Feb 2026, ~5% of LLM call spans errored and ~60% of those were rate-limit (HTTP 429) errors; March 2026 saw ~8.4M rate-limit errors. Provider capacity ceilings now directly compromise agent reliability — mitigate with budgeting + backpressure, not just prompt tweaks.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: Why is pass@1 a misleading reliability metric for long-horizon agents?
notes.back: Reliability degrades super-linearly with task complexity (duration × domain structure), and pass@1 on short atomic tasks hides this. Use variance-aware, duration-bucketed metrics like passk (τ-bench), ReliabilityBench, and METR task-completion horizons, with partial-credit scoring.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What does "91% of ML systems degrade over time" imply for agent operations?
notes.back: Reliability isn't a launch property — it decays (data drift, model/provider changes, dependency shifts). You need continuous monitoring, feedback loops, and proactive intervention, treating the agent like production software with ongoing evals, not a one-time deployment.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What must agent observability capture that traditional software observability doesn't?
notes.back: Because the LLM itself drives control flow, you must trace the model's decisions: per-request span tree with each tool call as a sub-span (tool name, latency, success flag, cost), guardrail verdicts, retrieval doc counts, and full trace IDs end-to-end — so non-deterministic paths are debuggable.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: In LLM-as-judge evaluation, why does the judge model's capability matter?
notes.back: Evaluator strength materially changes results: a strong judge (e.g. a 70B-class model) caught all known failures while smaller judges missed several cases. Weak judges give false confidence — budget for a capable evaluator (self-hosted is viable, ~sub-dollar per run in cited setups).

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: What hybrid architecture is emerging in 2026 for balancing capability and reliability?
notes.back: A guardrailed local model as the primary workhorse for routine structured tasks, with a frontier API as fallback for deep reasoning or very long context. Heavy guardrailing can push small models from ~50% to ~99% on bounded agentic workflows; the frontier handles the hard tail.

notes.deck: LLM, Agentic & Harness Engineering (2026)::05 Reliability & Evaluation (focus)
notes.front: Summarize the one-line reliability thesis for production agents.
notes.back: Models are strong; reliability comes from architecture + guardrails: strict tool contracts, deterministic/idempotent state transitions, trace-level observability, evals shipped in CI, and human approval for irreversible actions. Treat the agent as a distributed system where the LLM happens to be the planner/executor.
